why: Says blinding was not described, which is not a statement that nobody was blinded.

state.methods: The study was described as triple blind: patients, anaesthetists and the outcome assessors recording chronic pain and recurrence were unaware whether the mesh was fixed with tacks or with fibrin glue until the end of follow-up. The operating surgeon opened the sealed allocation envelope after induction of anaesthesia.

why: Patients and outcome assessors unaware; only the surgeon knew.

state.methods: After the index procedure, all patients underwent coronary CT angiography at 12 months, read by a core laboratory whose analysts were unaware of the assigned stent type. Patients and interventionalists were aware of the stent implanted.

why: Core lab analysts unaware; patients and interventionalists aware.

state.methods: Blinding was not performed. Participants were allocated to swimming training or to a land-based exercise programme; testing of VO2max was done by the same exercise physiologist before and after the intervention.

why: 'Blinding was not performed.'

state.methods: Participants were randomised to receive vitamin C 1 g/day or placebo for the winter season. Colds were self-recorded in a symptom diary. The randomisation code was held by the university pharmacy.

why: Placebo and a held code are described but no one is stated as blinded.

state.methods:
2.1 Study design
This was a 48-week, randomised, open-label, multicentre phase IIb study conducted at 27 hepatology centres in France, Belgium and Spain. Adults with biopsy-confirmed non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NAS ≥ 4, fibrosis stage F2-F3) were randomised 1:1:1 to oral pemafenor 0.4 mg once daily, pemafenor 0.8 mg once daily, or standard-of-care lifestyle counselling alone. Because the control arm received no study medication, participants and site investigators were aware of the assigned arm.
2.2 Histological assessment
Baseline and week-48 liver biopsies were read centrally by two expert hepatopathologists who were unaware of treatment arm, patient identity and biopsy sequence; disagreements were resolved by consensus. The primary endpoint was NASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis.
2.3 Safety
Adverse events were recorded at each visit by site investigators and coded with MedDRA v26.0. Liver stiffness was measured by vibration-controlled transient elastography at baseline and weeks 24 and 48.

why: Labelled open-label with aware participants and investigators, but central pathologists reading the primary endpoint were blinded.

state.methods: Participants received either an active hearing-protection earplug or a visually identical earplug without the acoustic filter. They were not told that there were two kinds of earplugs. Temporary threshold shift was measured by the investigator who handed out the earplugs.
state.study_type: occupational health crossover trial, sawmill workers

why: Workers unaware of two kinds; investigator measuring outcomes handed them out.

state.methods: The trial was open-label because the comparator was an intravenous formulation given in hospital while the investigational product was taken orally at home.
state.study_type: RCT, iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy

why: Open-label stated.

state.methods: Pain after tonsillectomy was assessed with the Parents' Postoperative Pain Measure by parents. Children aged 3-12 years were randomised to receive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg or ondansetron intraoperatively. Readmission for haemorrhage within 14 days was recorded.

why: No blinding stated for parents or anyone.

state.methods: Participants with fibromyalgia were randomised to nabilone or amitriptyline in a crossover design. To maintain blinding, both drugs were overencapsulated in identical capsules and an active placebo was not needed as both have sedative effects. Participants and the research nurse who conducted all assessments were blinded; only the hospital pharmacist knew the sequence.

why: Participants and assessing research nurse blinded.

state.methods: Patients were blinded. That is, patients received a sham intervention (detuned ultrasound) or real therapeutic ultrasound over the carpal tunnel. The outcome measures (Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire; nerve conduction) were obtained by the physiotherapist delivering the treatment.

why: Patients blinded via detuned ultrasound; the treating physiotherapist obtained outcomes.

state.methods: Neither the families nor the child psychiatrists were blinded, but the clinical global impression was rated by a separate psychiatrist who reviewed video recordings of the clinical interviews and was blinded to group (methylphenidate vs. behavioural parent training).

why: Only the separate video-rating psychiatrist was blinded.

state.methods: Data were collected at two hospitals using a pre-post design. In the 'before' period (Jan-Jun), usual care was delivered; in the 'after' period (Jul-Dec), a delirium prevention bundle was implemented. Delirium was screened twice daily by bedside nurses using the CAM-ICU.

why: No blinding mentioned.

state.methods: Patients with actinic keratoses on the face were randomised to daylight photodynamic therapy or cryotherapy. Clearance at 3 months was evaluated on standardised photographs by two dermatologists who were not informed of the treatment and had not treated the patients; patients were aware of which treatment they had undergone as the procedures are very different.

why: Photo-evaluating dermatologists uninformed; patients aware.

state.methods: The study was conducted in an unblinded manner. Participants in both groups were informed of the aims and procedures. Plasma lipids were analysed at an accredited laboratory.

why: Conducted 'unblinded'; an accredited lab is not stated as blinded, so nobody blinded.

state.methods: Participants were blind to condition. The experimental group listened to a 20-minute audio recording with embedded binaural beats at 10 Hz, and the control group listened to the same recording without the beat frequency difference; the recordings sounded the same to untrained listeners. Anxiety (STAI-S) was self-rated after listening.

why: Participants blind; outcome self-rated and no one else is stated as blinded.

state.methods: Patients were randomly allocated using a computer-generated table to either Group A (ultrasound-guided erector spinae block) or Group B (no block). Anesthesiologist administering general anaesthesia and the patient were blinded. Postoperative pain was assessed by a nurse who was unaware of group assignment. A sterile dressing was applied at the block site in both groups.

why: Patient, anaesthesiologist and the assessing nurse unaware.

state.methods: Participants were randomised to a smartphone-based gratitude journaling app or a neutral note-taking app. Well-being was measured with the WEMWBS at 4 weeks. Participants were compensated with a $20 gift card.

why: No blinding stated.

state.methods: Female footballers (n = 40) were randomised to the FIFA 11+ injury-prevention warm-up or a standard warm-up for one season. Coaches and players were not blinded to the warm-up programme. Injuries were recorded by team physiotherapists who were also aware of the allocation.

why: Coaches, players and the injury-recording physios aware.

state.methods: Single-blind. Patients undergoing colonoscopy were randomised to water exchange or air insufflation. Patients were sedated and did not know which method was used; endoscopists could not be blinded and recorded adenoma detection and cecal intubation time themselves.

why: Patients unaware; unblinded endoscopists recorded outcomes.

state.methods: Human pairwise judgments. For each prompt we sampled one output from the fine-tuned model and one from the base model and asked in-house annotators (n = 12) to pick the better one. Annotators were shown which output came from which model because the interface for this internal study displayed model identifiers.

why: The only people judging outcomes saw model identifiers, so nobody was blinded.

state.methods: Participants were unaware of their treatment allocation (hypertonic saline 7% vs isotonic saline 0.9%, delivered via nebuliser in identical ampoules). Lung clearance index was measured by respiratory physiologists blinded to allocation.

why: Participants and LCI-measuring physiologists blinded.

state.methods: Randomisation was performed with a 1:1 ratio by an online tool. Patients undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy had their appendiceal stump closed with either an endoloop or a stapler. Due to the design, blinding of the surgeons was not possible. Patients were not informed of the closure technique, and postoperative complications (intra-abdominal abscess, stump leak) were recorded by ward physicians who were unaware of it.

why: Surgeons unblinded, but patients were not told and ward physicians recording complications were unaware.

state.methods: Patients received the study drug (intranasal oxytocin 24 IU) or placebo spray. Both patients and their clinicians were blinded. Social responsiveness was rated by parents, who were also unaware of allocation.

why: Patients, clinicians and parent-raters blinded.

state.methods: Participants were told they would be taking part in one of two relaxation programmes and were not informed which one was the study intervention. Programme facilitators knew the allocation. The primary outcome, blood pressure, was measured at the programme venue by the facilitators with an automated cuff.

why: Participants not told which was the intervention; facilitators who measured BP knew.

state.methods: In this open-label randomised trial, adolescents with depression were assigned to fluoxetine plus CBT or fluoxetine alone. Outcome assessments using the CDRS-R were performed by independent evaluators masked to treatment assignment.

why: Open-label for patients, but evaluators were masked.

state.methods: Participants: 52 amateur runners. Intervention: 6 weeks of plyometric training (n=26) vs running only (n=26). Outcome: running economy at 12 km/h on a treadmill. Blinding: none (participants and testers knew groups).

why: 'Blinding: none'.

state.methods: Pigs were randomised to receive a novel haemostatic dressing or standard gauze after a standardised femoral artery injury. Blood loss was measured by weighing sponges, and survival at 3 h was recorded. Mean arterial pressure was maintained with a fixed fluid resuscitation protocol. The dressings were supplied by the manufacturer.

why: No blinding mentioned.

state.methods: Participants with dry eye disease were randomised to lifitegrast-like drops or vehicle eye drops, both supplied in identical single-use vials. Participants remained masked throughout the 12-week period. The site investigators were not masked, as they dispensed the vials from labelled cartons; corneal fluorescein staining was graded by these investigators.

why: Participants masked; grading investigators not.

state.methods: Study nurses measuring blood pressure were blinded to intervention status, as the salt substitute sachets and the regular salt sachets were identical and distributed by village health workers. Households were told they were receiving a free salt supply and were not told there were two types.

why: Households not told there were two types (participant blinding) and BP nurses blinded.

state.methods: Given the behavioural nature of the intervention (motivational interviewing delivered by trained counsellors vs. a leaflet), participants and counsellors were aware of allocation. We did not blind outcome assessment: follow-up interviews at 6 months were done by the study coordinator, who also performed randomisation.

why: Participants, counsellors and outcome assessment all unblinded.

state.study_type: phase III RCT, oncology supportive care
state.methods: Patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy were randomised to olanzapine 5 mg or placebo on days 1-4, in addition to standard antiemetic prophylaxis. Olanzapine and placebo tablets were identical. Patients were blinded to their assignment. Nausea was self-reported on a 0-10 scale in a daily diary, which was reviewed by the treating oncology nurse, who had access to the pharmacy dispensing record.

why: Patients blinded; outcome self-reported and the reviewing nurse had access to allocation.

state.methods: The volunteers were exposed for 2 h to either filtered air or diesel exhaust (300 µg/m³ PM2.5) in an exposure chamber, in random order, 4 weeks apart. Bronchoalveolar lavage was performed 6 h after each exposure.

why: No blinding stated.

state.methods: A research assistant not involved in recruitment or treatment, and blinded to group allocation, performed all baseline and follow-up measurements (6MWT, 30-second chair stand, SPPB). Participants were randomised to a home-based exercise programme with weekly phone coaching or a leaflet on physical activity.

why: Only the measuring RA was blinded; participants know if they exercise with coaching.

state.methods: Blinding: The participants were blinded to group allocation by use of a placebo manipulation (hands-on contact without thrust). Due to the nature of the manipulation, the clinician could not be blinded. The assessor was not blinded and was the same clinician.

why: Participants blinded; clinician-assessor explicitly not.

state.methods: Preschools were randomised to a 12-week dialogic reading programme or business as usual. Both teachers and parents knew which condition their preschool was in, and the vocabulary tests (PPVT-4) at post-test were administered by research staff who were aware of condition because they also conducted classroom fidelity observations.

why: Teachers, parents and testers all aware.

state.methods: Each patient with bilateral knee osteoarthritis received platelet-rich plasma in one knee and saline in the other (randomised side). Patients were blinded to which knee received PRP. Assessments of each knee (VAS, KOOS subscale per knee) were made by the patient.

why: Patients blinded; no other blinding described and patients self-assessed.

state.methods: All participants received the same number of weekly group sessions. Group assignment (acceptance and commitment therapy vs. relaxation training) was determined by randomisation. Tinnitus Handicap Inventory scores were collected at baseline, post-treatment and at 6 months.

why: No blinding stated.

state.methods: Open-label design. Patients were randomised to self-administered subcutaneous methotrexate at home or oral methotrexate. Disease activity (DAS28) was assessed by a joint assessor who was not blinded to treatment route.

why: Open-label and the joint assessor not blinded.

state.methods: The two statisticians who performed the primary analysis worked on a dataset in which the treatment groups were labelled X and Y; the code was broken only after the primary analysis was finalised and the interpretation agreed. The trial compared a four-week intensive outpatient smoking cessation clinic with a single advice session.

why: Only analysts were blinded; clinic vs single advice session is unblindable for participants.

state.methods: Participants (bodybuilders, n = 18) were given capsules containing either beta-alanine (6.4 g/d) or placebo. Paraesthesia, a common side effect of beta-alanine, was reported by most participants in the beta-alanine group. Muscle carnosine was measured by 1H-MRS.

why: Placebo capsules and a side effect threatening the blind are discussed, but blinding itself is never stated.

state.methods: Patients with temporomandibular disorder were randomised to low-level laser therapy or placebo laser (the device emitted the same sound and light indicator but the laser diode was disconnected). Both the patients and the examiner who performed the palpation and mouth-opening measurements were blinded; the operator who applied the laser was the only person who knew the allocation.

why: Patients and examiner blinded; only the operator knew.

state.methods: No blinding of participants or personnel was possible. Outcome assessment was blinded in part: the radiographic union assessment was performed by an independent radiologist blinded to allocation, but the functional scores were collected by the unblinded study surgeon. The primary outcome was radiographic union at 6 months.

why: A radiologist assessing the primary outcome was blinded; participants and personnel were not.

state.methods: Adults with obesity were randomised to a commercial weight-loss programme or a GP-led brief intervention. Weight was measured at 12 months by a research nurse at the participant's GP practice.

why: Blinding not mentioned.

state.methods: Participants were blinded to allocation to real or sham mirror therapy (sham: covered mirror with a verbal explanation that the covered condition was a 'visualisation variant'). The therapist who ran all sessions also administered the Fugl-Meyer Assessment and was unblinded.

why: Participants blinded; therapist-assessor unblinded.

state.methods: This was an open study. Patients were aware they received either the new tablet formulation of the antiepileptic or the syrup formulation. Seizure frequency was recorded by patients and caregivers in paper diaries.

why: Open study; patients aware; self-recorded outcomes.

state.methods: Participants (n = 180, recruited via an online panel) evaluated 40 loan applications each with the help of an AI model and were randomised to see either feature-attribution explanations or no explanation alongside the model's recommendation. Decision accuracy was computed automatically against ground truth; trust was measured with a 7-item scale.

why: No blinding stated.

state.methods: Masking: participants, investigators and outcome assessors were masked to group assignment. The intervention (prophylactic azithromycin 2 g single oral dose in labour) and placebo were prepared as identical suspensions by the manufacturer.

why: Participants, investigators and outcome assessors masked.

state.methods: Participants were blinded to the type of ice cream they received (full-sugar vs. an allulose-sweetened version matched for taste and texture). The researchers conducting the glucose tolerance tests prepared the portions in the lab kitchen before each visit.

why: Participants blinded; researchers who prepared portions ran the tests and so were not blinded.

state.methods: Because the intervention consisted of a group dance class, it was not possible to blind the participants. The assessor administering the Berg Balance Scale was not aware of the group allocation, and participants were reminded not to disclose their group.
state.study_type: falls prevention RCT, older women, Korea

why: Participants unblinded; assessor unaware.

state.methods: Open-label, randomised, two-period crossover bioequivalence study in 36 healthy volunteers comparing a generic and the reference formulation of tacrolimus 5 mg. Plasma concentrations were determined by a validated LC-MS/MS method.

why: Open-label stated.

state.methods: Patients with plantar heel pain were randomised to custom foot orthoses or sham orthoses (flat insoles of the same material). Patients were not told which insole was 'real'. Foot Function Index scores were recorded by a podiatrist who was independent of the orthosis fitting and blinded to allocation.

why: Patients not told and the independent podiatrist-assessor blinded.

state.methods: Children with nocturnal enuresis were randomised to an enuresis alarm or desmopressin. Wet nights were recorded by parents in a diary over 12 weeks. The study was conducted in five paediatric outpatient clinics in Turkey.

why: No blinding stated.

state.methods: Single blind (participant). Participants in the control group received a vibrating foam roller with the motor switched off, while the experimental group used it switched on at 33 Hz; participants were told the study compared 'two roller settings'. Hamstring flexibility (sit-and-reach) was measured by the investigator supervising the rolling.

why: Single blind (participant); the supervising investigator measured outcomes.

state.methods: The trial had no masking. Couples undergoing IVF were randomised to single blastocyst transfer or double cleavage-stage embryo transfer; clinicians, embryologists and couples knew the number of embryos transferred.

why: 'No masking'; everyone knew.

state.methods: Statistical analysis. The primary outcome, change in systolic blood pressure from baseline to week 12, was analysed using ANCOVA with treatment group as a fixed factor and baseline systolic pressure and study site as covariates. Missing week-12 values were handled by multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption (20 imputed datasets). Secondary continuous outcomes were analysed in the same way.
state.primary_outcome: Change in seated office systolic BP at week 12

why: Primary outcome analysed by ANCOVA adjusting for baseline.

state.methods: Data were entered into Microsoft Excel, cleaned, and exported to SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) for analysis. Results are presented as frequencies, percentages, means and standard deviations. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
state.primary_outcome: Proportion of mothers exclusively breastfeeding at 6 months

why: Only software and a significance threshold; no test for the primary outcome.

state.study: Cluster-randomised trial of a structured phonics programme in 42 primary schools (Kenya, Kisumu county)
state.methods: The primary outcome (oral reading fluency, correct words per minute at endline) was modelled with a two-level linear model, pupils nested in schools, with arm as a school-level fixed effect and baseline fluency as a pupil-level covariate. Random intercepts for school. Estimation by restricted maximum likelihood in Stata 17 (mixed).

why: Primary outcome: two-level linear mixed model with random school intercepts.

state.methods: All analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle by a statistician blinded to group allocation. Appropriate statistical tests were applied depending on the distribution of the data. Two-sided p<0.05 was considered significant.
state.primary_outcome: Time to first COPD exacerbation requiring oral corticosteroids

why: 'Appropriate statistical tests' is generic; nothing named for time-to-exacerbation.

state.methods:
2.6 Statistical analysis
Time from randomisation to disease progression or death (PFS) was compared between arms with a stratified log-rank test (strata: ECOG 0 vs 1, prior lines 1 vs 2+). Hazard ratios with 95% CIs were estimated from a Cox proportional hazards model with the same stratification factors. Proportional hazards were checked with Schoenfeld residuals.

why: PFS analysed by stratified log-rank test and Cox model.

state.methods: Baseline characteristics of the two groups were compared using independent-samples t-tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Groups were well balanced. The primary outcome, pain intensity on the 0-10 NRS at 6 weeks, was compared between the intervention and usual-care groups and is reported as mean difference with 95% confidence interval.

why: t-tests and chi-square are named only for baseline balance; the primary comparison names no test.

state.methods: Seedling survival (alive/dead at day 120) was the response variable. We fitted binomial generalized linear mixed models (logit link) with canopy treatment, herbivore exclusion and their interaction as fixed effects and plot nested within block as random intercepts, using glmmTMB in R 4.3.2. Significance of fixed effects was assessed by likelihood-ratio tests.

why: Survival analysed with binomial GLMM plus likelihood-ratio tests.

state.methods: Sample size: assuming a standard deviation of 8 points and a minimal important difference of 5 points on the KOOS pain subscale, 45 participants per group provide 80% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 using a two-sample t-test, allowing 15% attrition. Analysis: KOOS pain at 12 months will be compared between groups as described in the statistical analysis plan, which will be finalised before database lock.

why: The t-test appears only in the power calculation; the analysis itself is deferred to an unpublished SAP.

state.methods: Participants rated each pair of model responses (A vs B, order randomised) for overall helpfulness. The primary metric was the win rate of System B over System A, with ties split evenly. We tested whether the win rate differed from 50% with a two-sided exact binomial test over non-tied judgments, and report Wilson 95% intervals.
state.primary_outcome: Pairwise win rate, System B vs System A

why: Primary win rate tested with an exact binomial test.

state.methods: Statistical analysis was conducted using SAS 9.4. The primary efficacy variable (HbA1c change from baseline at week 26) was analysed with PROC MIXED, including treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction and baseline HbA1c as fixed effects and an unstructured covariance matrix for repeated measures within patient.

why: PROC MIXED with repeated-measures covariance is a named mixed model (MMRM), even though framed as software.

state.methods: Continuous variables are reported as median (IQR) and categorical variables as n (%). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. All analyses were done in R (version 4.2.1).

why: Descriptive summaries, threshold and software only.

state.design: prospective cohort, 11,204 adults, Guangzhou Biobank sub-sample
state.methods: Incident type 2 diabetes was ascertained through linkage to hospital and primary-care records. Person-years were counted from enrolment until diagnosis, death, emigration or 31 Dec 2021. Associations of baseline sleep duration categories with incident diabetes were estimated using Cox proportional hazards regression with age as the time scale, adjusted for sex, education, BMI, smoking and physical activity.

why: Incident diabetes (the outcome) analysed with Cox regression.

state.methods: Normality of continuous variables was assessed with the Shapiro-Wilk test and homogeneity of variance with Levene's test. Where assumptions were violated, data were log-transformed. Differences in the primary outcome between groups were then evaluated and considered significant at p<0.05.

why: Shapiro-Wilk and Levene are assumption checks; the test for the primary between-group difference is never named.

state.methods: Because the primary endpoint (proportion achieving ACR20 at week 24) is binary, the difference between arms was tested with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratified by region and baseline methotrexate use. Patients who discontinued before week 24 were counted as non-responders.

why: ACR20 proportion compared with a stratified CMH test.

state.methods: Yield (t/ha, adjusted to 14% moisture) was analysed as a split-plot ANOVA with irrigation regime as the main plot and nitrogen rate as the sub-plot, in a randomised complete block design with four replicates. Means were separated with Tukey's HSD at alpha = 0.05.

why: Yield analysed by split-plot ANOVA.

state.methods: Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Inferential statistics were used to determine whether differences observed between the experimental and control classes were statistically significant. Data analysis was carried out with the aid of the Statistical Package for Social Sciences.

why: 'Inferential statistics' and SPSS, no specific test.

state.methods: Continuous outcomes were compared with Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test, and categorical outcomes with the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate.

why: The categorical-outcome mapping (chi-square/Fisher) clearly covers the binary primary outcome.

state.methods: We estimate the effect of the minimum-wage increase on teen employment using a difference-in-differences design comparing treated counties with contiguous cross-border counties. Our baseline specification is a two-way fixed-effects regression of log employment on the treatment indicator with county-pair-by-quarter and county fixed effects; standard errors are clustered at the state level.

why: Two-way fixed-effects DiD regression named for the main outcome.

state.methods: Secondary outcomes (number of emergency visits, number of hospital admissions) were analysed with negative binomial regression with log follow-up time as offset. Quality-of-life scores were compared using mixed models. The primary outcome is described descriptively in Table 2 with between-group differences and 95% CIs.
state.primary_outcome: Days alive and out of hospital at 90 days

why: Models are named for secondary outcomes only; the primary is 'described descriptively' without a test or model.

state.methods: Participants completed the 12-item scale before and after the 8-week mindfulness course. Pre-post change in total perceived stress was assessed with a paired-samples t-test; effect size is reported as Cohen's d(z).

why: Pre-post primary change tested with a paired t-test.

state.methods: Statistical methods: The study was analysed on a per-protocol basis. Statistical tests used were two-tailed. The level of significance was 5%. Analyses were done with GraphPad Prism 9.
state.primary_outcome: Postoperative nausea and vomiting within 24 h

why: Only 'two-tailed tests', alpha and software.

state.methods: The primary analysis uses a Bayesian hierarchical logistic model for 28-day mortality, with random effects for site and for the nine variant-specific domains, weakly informative priors N(0, 1.5^2) on log-odds ratios, and posterior probability of benefit (OR < 1) > 0.99 as the efficacy threshold.

why: Bayesian hierarchical logistic model for 28-day mortality.

state.methods: Task completion time (s) was log-transformed. Because each participant used all three interfaces, we used a repeated-measures ANOVA with interface as the within-subject factor, with Greenhouse-Geisser correction; post-hoc comparisons used Holm-corrected paired t-tests. Error counts and SUS scores are reported descriptively.

why: Completion time analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA.

state.methods: Multivariable analysis was used to adjust for potential confounders (age, sex, Charlson index, admission ward). Variables with p<0.2 in univariable analysis were entered into the multivariable analysis. Results are presented with 95% confidence intervals.

why: 'Multivariable analysis' with no model type; the regression family is never named.

state.methods: Number of wild bee visits per 10-minute observation was the response. Counts were overdispersed (dispersion ratio 3.4), so we used a negative binomial GLMM with flower strip treatment and survey round as fixed effects and farm as a random intercept.

why: Visitation counts analysed with a negative binomial GLMM.

state.methods:
2.8. Statistical analysis
The analysis population comprised all randomised participants (modified ITT: at least one dose of study drug). Demographic and baseline characteristics were summarised by treatment arm. For the primary endpoint, the proportion of participants with sustained virological response 12 weeks after end of treatment (SVR12), point estimates and two-sided 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each arm. Participants with missing SVR12 data were considered failures. Safety data were tabulated by system organ class and preferred term (MedDRA v25.0). All analyses were performed with SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).

why: Only per-arm point estimates and CIs; no test or model compares SVR12 between arms.

state.methods: Statistical analysis was performed by using standard methods. The data were expressed as mean ± SEM. Differences were regarded as significant at P < .05.
state.primary_outcome: Infarct size (% of area at risk) in mice

why: 'Standard methods' names nothing.

state.methods: The primary outcome was analysed using a linear mixed-effects model including all post-randomisation time points (6 weeks, 3 and 6 months), with fixed effects for arm, time, arm x time and baseline PHQ-9, and a random intercept for participant and for therapist (to account for clustering in the intervention arm only, using a partially nested specification). The treatment effect at 6 months was estimated from the arm x time contrast.

why: PHQ-9 analysed with a linear mixed-effects model.

state.methods: The primary analysis will follow the approach used in our pilot trial (Hosseini et al., 2021), with adjustment for the minimisation variables. Secondary analyses will explore effect modification by baseline severity.

state.methods:
Statistical analysis
The full analysis set included all randomised participants who received at least one dose. The primary endpoint, change from baseline in the weekly average of daily worst itch NRS at week 16, was analysed using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, baseline NRS and baseline NRS-by-visit interaction as fixed effects and region as a stratification factor. Data collected after use of rescue medication were set to missing. Type I error across the primary and key secondary endpoints was controlled with a fixed-sequence procedure. state.methods: Statistical analysis. Descriptive statistics summarised the sample. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test indicated non-normal distributions for most variables; therefore non-parametric tests were used.
state.primary_outcome: Burnout score, nurses on night shifts vs day shifts

why: Only the normality test is named; 'non-parametric tests' is a category, not a named test.

state.methods:
3.4 Data analysis
Interview data (n = 18 teachers) were analysed thematically. For the quantitative strand, the student survey (n = 1,146; 38 classes) included the 12-item Belonging in Class scale administered in September and again in May. Item-level missing data were below 2% and were handled by person-mean imputation when at least 10 of 12 items were answered. Scale scores were computed as the item mean (range 1-5). Class-level averages were calculated for the 19 classes that used the restorative-circle routine and the 19 that did not, and the change between September and May is displayed in Figure 2, separately for students who were new to the school and those continuing. We interpret differences of 0.2 or more on the scale mean as practically meaningful, based on the scale developers' guidance. All analyses were conducted in R 4.3.1.
state.primary_outcome: Change in sense of belonging (Sep to May)

why: Detailed data preparation, but the change is only displayed and read against a practical threshold; no test or model.

state.methods: The effect of the nurse-led follow-up on 30-day readmission was estimated with a generalised estimating equation (logit link, exchangeable correlation) to account for clustering of patients within wards.

why: GEE logistic model for readmission.

state.methods: Unless stated otherwise, data are reported as mean ± standard error of three independent biological replicates. Significance thresholds: ns, p ≥ 0.05; *, p < 0.05; **, p < 0.01.
state.primary_outcome: Relative expression of the drought-responsive gene

why: Significance markers without a test.

state.methods: Change in total Montreal Cognitive Assessment score from baseline to 18 months was compared between the multidomain intervention and health-advice arms using a constrained longitudinal data analysis (cLDA) model with baseline included as part of the response vector.

why: cLDA is a named longitudinal model, though less familiar than ANCOVA or MMRM.

state.methods: Data were double-checked by two investigators, and all analyses were performed after the database was locked. The primary outcome (sustained ventricular tachycardia at 12 months) was analysed as the proportion of patients free from events.
state.primary_outcome: Freedom from sustained VT at 12 months

why: The outcome definition is restated with no method.

state.methods: Household monthly consumption expenditure per adult equivalent (log) was regressed on the cash transfer eligibility indicator using an ANCOVA specification (endline outcome on treatment and baseline outcome) with district fixed effects, as pre-specified in the pre-analysis plan.

why: ANCOVA regression specification on log consumption.

state.methods: The research used a mixed-methods approach. Quantitative data were analysed statistically and qualitative data thematically. Triangulation of findings strengthened the validity of the conclusions.

why: 'Analysed statistically' names nothing.

state.methods: Recovery of the pre-disturbance bird community was assessed with permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, 9,999 permutations) comparing logged, burned and intact sites.

why: PERMANOVA on community composition.

state.methods: Baseline characteristics are reported by arm without significance testing, in line with CONSORT. The intervention effect on the primary outcome is estimated as described in the published statistical analysis plan (doi:10.xxxx/sap.2022.041).

why: Defers to a SAP by DOI; no method named here.

state.methods: Customer satisfaction (CSAT 1-5) after the chatbot vs human-agent interaction was compared with an ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds) adjusting for issue category and customer tenure.

why: Proportional odds model on CSAT.

state.methods: Of 412 participants randomised, 389 completed the 12-week assessment. Mean systolic blood pressure fell by 9.1 mmHg with the salt substitute and 4.3 mmHg with regular salt. The between-group difference was statistically and clinically significant. Adverse events were rare and similar between groups.
state.primary_outcome: Change in systolic BP at 12 weeks

why: Claims significance without a named test.

state.methods: The primary outcome was total nights with bed-wetting in the last 14 nights of treatment. We compared groups using a Poisson regression; because variance exceeded the mean, a negative binomial model is reported.

why: Negative binomial regression for wet nights.

state.methods: Inclusion criteria: adults aged 18-65 with chronic neck pain > 3 months. Exclusion: prior cervical surgery, red flags, pregnancy. Outcome measures were collected at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks by an assessor blinded to group. Analyses were performed with SPSS 25 at alpha = 0.05.

why: Eligibility, timing and software; no test.

state.methods: Two-sample t-tests were used to compare secondary continuous outcomes (satisfaction, anxiety). Chi-square tests were used for secondary categorical outcomes. For the primary outcome, see the non-inferiority analysis in Section 2.7.
state.primary_outcome: Successful IV cannulation on first attempt

why: Tests are explicitly for secondary outcomes; the primary analysis is in a section not shown.

state.methods: Seed germination (%) after 14 days was arcsine-square-root transformed and analysed by one-way ANOVA across the six priming treatments, with means separated by Tukey's HSD.

why: One-way ANOVA on germination.

state.methods: Results of the primary outcome analysis should be interpreted in the light of the lower than expected event rate. Post hoc power was 42%. Differences between groups were not statistically significant, as shown by the overlapping confidence intervals.

why: Post hoc power and CI overlap; no test named.

state.methods: We measured user reliance on the AI suggestion (accepting it when it was wrong). Participants (n = 212) completed 30 trials each. The primary analysis was a GLMM with a binomial family: accept_wrong ~ explanation_condition + (1 | participant) + (1 | item).

why: Binomial GLMM on over-reliance.

state.methods: We relied on nonparametric statistics throughout because of the small sample.
state.primary_outcome: Change in forced vital capacity after 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (n = 14)

why: 'Nonparametric statistics' is a family, not a named test.

state.methods: Pupils' writing quality was scored on a 6-trait rubric. Because only 8 classes were randomised, we used a randomisation (permutation) test on class-level mean scores, re-randomising allocation 10,000 times.

why: Permutation test on class-mean writing scores.

state.methods: Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value of the rapid antigen test were calculated against RT-PCR as the reference standard, with 95% CIs.
state.primary_outcome: Sensitivity of rapid antigen test vs RT-PCR

why: Accuracy metrics with CIs are computed but no test or model is named for sensitivity.

state.methods: Monthly housing rent (log, per m²) was modelled with a hedonic regression including dwelling characteristics, neighbourhood fixed effects and a post-rent-control indicator interacted with a covered-unit indicator.

why: Hedonic regression on log rent.

state.methods: The research instrument was a structured questionnaire, and a four-point Likert scale was used. Mean scores of 2.50 and above were regarded as agreed, while below 2.50 were regarded as disagreed.

why: Cut-off rule on means, no test.

state.methods: The co-primary outcome of time to first acute chest syndrome episode was analysed with a Cox proportional hazards model; the other co-primary outcome, annual rate of vaso-occlusive crises, with a negative binomial model with exposure time as offset.
state.primary_outcome: Time to first ACS; annual VOC rate

why: Both co-primaries have named models (Cox, negative binomial).

state.methods: Data were imported into NVivo 14 and analysed. Descriptive frequency counts of attendance and satisfaction were compiled from the programme register.

why: Frequency counts only.

state.methods: We compare the accuracy of the fine-tuned and base models on the 1,000-question held-out set with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals; the fine-tuned model is considered better when its interval lies entirely above the base model's.

why: Non-overlapping bootstrap CIs is a decision rule, not a named test or model.

state.methods: 2.4 Sample size. Assuming a difference of 1.0 point in the primary outcome (Oxford Knee Score at 12 months) between the injection and physiotherapy arms, a standard deviation of 2.2, two-sided alpha of 0.05 and 90% power, 103 participants per arm were required. Allowing for 15% loss to follow-up, we aimed to randomise 242 participants.

why: Full power calculation with effect size, SD, alpha and power.

state.methods: Participants. Forty-eight undergraduates (31 women, 17 men; mean age = 19.8, SD = 1.6) from a large Midwestern university participated in exchange for course credit. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Two participants were excluded for failing the attention check, leaving a final sample of 46.

why: Only reports N and demographics; nothing on how 48 was chosen.

state.methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with community pharmacists in Leinster between March and July 2022. Interviews were analysed concurrently using reflexive thematic analysis, and recruitment continued until no new codes emerged in three consecutive interviews, at which point we judged data saturation to have been reached (n = 17).

why: Explicit saturation stopping rule determined the number of interviews.

state.methods: The sample size was determined a priori. A total of 120 patients undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy were randomly allocated (1:1) to receive either ondansetron 4 mg or dexamethasone 8 mg at induction.

why: 'Determined a priori' says when, not how; no calculation or rationale is given.

state.methods:
Study sites and sampling
Fieldwork took place in 14 permanent plots (1 ha each) across the Białowieża lowland forest. Within each plot we sampled all standing deadwood > 10 cm DBH. The number of plots was fixed by the existing long-term monitoring network, which comprises exactly these 14 plots; no additional plots could be established under the park's permit.

why: The number of plots was set by the existing monitoring network and permit, which is a stated reason for the size.

state.methods: Sample size was calculated with G*Power 3.1 for a repeated-measures ANOVA (within-between interaction) with 2 groups and 3 measurements. Assuming a medium effect (f = 0.25), α = .05, 1-β = .80 and a correlation among repeated measures of .5, the required total sample was 28. To account for dropout we recruited 34 recreational runners.

why: G*Power calculation with effect size, alpha and power stated.

state.methods: Consistent with previous studies in this area (e.g., Hartley et al., 2017; Moreno & Ruiz, 2019), we recruited 24 participants per condition. Participants were native Spanish speakers tested at the university laboratory.

why: Bare appeal to prior studies' sample sizes with no stated rationale (counted as false).

state.methods: Human evaluation. We sampled 400 system outputs uniformly at random from the test set (100 per system). Each output was rated for fluency and faithfulness on a 5-point Likert scale by three annotators recruited via a crowdsourcing platform and paid above the local minimum wage. Inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's α) was 0.61.

why: Gives counts of outputs and raters but no reason for 400.

state.methods: Sample size. The primary objective was to estimate the prevalence of hypertension among adults aged 30–69 in the district. Assuming an expected prevalence of 25%, a desired precision of ±3 percentage points, a 95% confidence level and a design effect of 1.5 for the two-stage cluster design, the required sample was 1,201; this was inflated to 1,340 to allow for a 10% non-response rate.

why: Precision-based calculation with expected prevalence, margin and design effect.

state.methods: Animals: Male C57BL/6J mice (8–10 weeks, n = 10 per group) were obtained from an accredited supplier and housed 4 per cage under a 12 h light/dark cycle with food and water ad libitum. All procedures were approved by the institutional animal ethics committee (protocol AE-2021-044).

why: Group size stated without any reason.

state.methods: The trial was powered on the secondary outcome of 6-minute walk distance rather than on the primary outcome (hospital readmission), because readmission rates in the pilot were too low to allow a feasible sample. Detecting a 30 m difference (SD 70 m) with 80% power at α = 0.05 required 86 per group; 190 were randomised.

why: Power calculation exists (on a secondary outcome); it still states how the sample size was chosen.

state.methods: Participants were 212 Year 7 students from six state secondary schools in Queensland who returned signed parental consent. Schools were recruited through the regional education office. Classes were randomly assigned to the retrieval-practice condition or business-as-usual instruction.

why: Recruitment described, sample size not justified.

state.methods: Based on the effect observed in our pilot study (Cohen's d = 0.62, n = 20), we estimated that 42 participants would be needed to detect an effect of that size with 80% power in a paired t-test (two-tailed, α = .05). We preregistered a target of 50 to allow for exclusions.

why: Pilot effect size fed into a power calculation.

state.methods: Post hoc sensitivity analysis. With the final sample of 63 participants, α = .05 and power of .80, the smallest effect our design could reliably detect was d = 0.36. Participants were recruited through Prolific over one weekend in April 2023.

why: Sensitivity analysis after the fact describes detectable effects, not how the sample size was chosen.

state.methods: All consecutive adult patients presenting to the emergency department of Hospital Universitario San Rafael with suspected sepsis between 1 January 2019 and 31 December 2020 were eligible. Because the aim was to describe the full two-year case mix after the introduction of the qSOFA screening protocol, no sample size calculation was performed and all eligible patients in the period were included (n = 1,487).

why: Explains that the whole eligible population over the protocol period was included and why; that is a stated basis.

state.methods: Eighty-two children aged 4–6 years were recruited from kindergartens in Taipei. Children were tested individually in a quiet room at their school by one of two trained experimenters, in two sessions of about 20 minutes each.

why: N only.

state.methods:
Sample size
We used a Bayesian sequential design with a maximum N. Data collection continued in batches of 20 until the Bayes factor for the key contrast exceeded 10 in either direction or N reached 200. Collection stopped at N = 140 (BF10 = 11.3). The stopping rule was preregistered on OSF.

why: Preregistered sequential stopping rule determined N.

state.methods: We ran the experiment in 60 villages in Kakamega County, randomly assigning 30 to receive unconditional cash transfers. Within each village, 12 households were selected at random from the census list compiled by the field team.

why: Villages and households counted, no justification given.

state.methods: A power analysis indicated that 60 participants would provide adequate power to detect the expected interaction. Sixty-four participants took part; data from four were lost due to equipment failure.

why: Names a power analysis as the basis, even though parameters are missing.

state.methods: Group size was determined using the resource equation approach (Mead's E), which is recommended for exploratory animal studies where no prior effect size estimate is available; with 4 groups, n = 6 per group gives E = 20, the upper bound of the acceptable range.

why: Resource equation method stated as the basis for group size.

state.methods: Statistical power was maximised by using a fully within-subject design in which every participant completed all six conditions. Twenty-two right-handed adults (age 21–34) took part, recruited from the departmental participant pool.

why: Mentions power only as a design feature; says nothing about how 22 was chosen.

state.methods: Participants and design. Healthy, physically active males (n = 12; age 24 ± 3 y; VO2max 55.1 ± 4.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) completed three trials in randomised, counterbalanced order: placebo, 3 mg·kg⁻¹ caffeine and 6 mg·kg⁻¹ caffeine. Trials were separated by at least 7 days.

why: No statement of how 12 was chosen.

state.methods: Sample size: 30 patients per arm, following the widely cited recommendation of at least 12 per group for pilot trials (Julious, 2005), increased to 30 to allow estimation of the recruitment and retention rates with a 95% CI half-width of roughly ±15%. The purpose of the pilot is to inform the design of a definitive trial, not to test efficacy.

why: Pilot-trial rule of thumb plus a precision target for feasibility rates.

state.methods: Methods — Dietary assessment. A total of 356 women from the Nord-Trøndelag cohort completed two non-consecutive 24-h recalls and a validated 180-item FFQ. Energy intake was adjusted using the residual method. Misreporters were identified with the Goldberg cut-off.

why: N stated without any rationale.

state.methods: The number of annotators and items was chosen to match the evaluation protocol of the shared task organisers, who specify 200 items and 3 annotators per item so that system rankings are comparable across submissions.

why: Follows a convention but states the reason (comparability under the shared-task protocol).

state.methods: Sample size and power. The unit of randomisation was the general practice. Based on routine data from the 2019 audit, we expected 38% of eligible patients in control practices to have an HbA1c recorded below 58 mmol/mol at 12 months. To detect an absolute increase of 10 percentage points with 85% power and a two-sided α of 0.05, assuming an average cluster size of 45 eligible patients and an intracluster correlation coefficient of 0.05 (taken from a previous primary care trial in the same region), 32 practices (16 per arm) were needed. We planned to recruit 36 practices to protect against practice withdrawal, which in our previous trials has been around 10%. The ICC was re-estimated at the interim data-monitoring meeting without unblinding, and no adjustment to the target was required.

why: Cluster-adjusted power calculation with ICC, effect size, alpha and power.

state.methods: We interviewed 40 small-scale fishers in four landing sites along the Kenyan coast (Shimoni, Vanga, Gazi and Kibuyuni), ten per site. Interviews were conducted in Kiswahili by a local research assistant and lasted 30–60 minutes.

why: Numbers per site given, no reason for them.

state.methods:
2.2 Participants
A sample size of 128 (64 per group) was required to detect a medium effect (d = 0.5) on post-test reading fluency with 80% power, α = .05, two-tailed (independent-samples t-test). We recruited 141 second-grade pupils from nine primary schools in the Flemish region of Belgium.

why: Explicit power calculation for the primary outcome.

state.methods: This was a retrospective cohort study. Electronic health records of 9,412 patients who initiated a DPP-4 inhibitor or a sulfonylurea as second-line therapy between 2012 and 2018 were extracted from the regional database. Follow-up was censored at treatment switch, death, emigration or 31 December 2020.

why: Describes which records were extracted but gives no reason for the period or size; no sample size basis stated.

state.methods: Sample size was based on the recommendation of Nielsen and Landauer that five users uncover roughly 85% of usability problems in a formative test; we ran two rounds of five participants, one before and one after the redesign of the checkout flow.

why: States the five-user heuristic and its rationale as the basis.

state.methods: Rats (Sprague-Dawley, male, 250–300 g) were randomly assigned to sham, vehicle or treatment groups (n = 8/group). This group size was based on our previous experience with this model.

why: 'Based on our previous experience' is a bare appeal to habit with no stated effect size, variance or rationale.

state.methods: Group size was calculated from our previous study with this model (Ferreira et al., 2020), in which infarct volume was 38 ± 9% in vehicle-treated animals. To detect a 30% relative reduction (to 26.6%) with 80% power at α = 0.05 (two-sided t-test), 8 animals per group were required; 10 per group were allocated to allow for peri-operative mortality of up to 20%.

why: Power calculation using SD from a prior study.

state.methods: Participants. We recruited as many participants as possible from the department's subject pool during the spring 2022 semester. The final sample comprised 157 students (112 female) aged 18–26.

why: Explicit stopping rule (as many as possible within one semester) is a stated, if weak, basis for N.

state.methods: The survey was distributed to all 2,650 registered nurses employed by the three participating health boards via the staff intranet, with two email reminders. 814 completed questionnaires were returned (response rate 30.7%).

why: Describes a census invitation and response rate, but not why this population or any target size; no stated basis.

state.methods: sample size: n=24 (power analysis in supplement).
state.notes: Excerpt from a short communication; the supplement itself was not provided with the manuscript.

why: Tells the reader N came from a power analysis, even though details are elsewhere.

state.methods: Participants (N = 300) were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and paid $1.50 for a 10-minute study. Only workers located in the United States with an approval rating of at least 95% were eligible. We excluded 27 participants who failed one or more attention checks.

why: No justification for 300.

state.methods: For the model development cohort, we targeted at least 10 outcome events per candidate predictor. With 14 candidate predictors and an anticipated 30-day mortality of 12%, this required roughly 1,170 patients; the registry provided 1,532 eligible admissions over the study window.

why: Events-per-variable rule stated as the basis.

state.methods: Material y métodos. Se incluyeron 64 pacientes con diagnóstico de fibromialgia según los criterios ACR 2016, atendidos en la Unidad de Reumatología entre enero y octubre de 2021. Los pacientes fueron asignados aleatoriamente a hidroterapia o a ejercicio en seco.

why: Gives N and recruitment period only.

state.methods: Tamaño muestral: considerando una diferencia mínima clínicamente relevante de 1,5 puntos en la escala EVA del dolor, una desviación estándar de 2,4, un riesgo alfa de 0,05 y una potencia del 80% en un contraste bilateral, se requerían 41 pacientes por grupo. Asumiendo un 10% de pérdidas, se reclutaron 46 por grupo.

why: Power calculation with MCID, SD, alpha and power.

state.methods: We used all 1,850 prompts from the public benchmark's held-out split. For each prompt, two model responses were shown side by side to one of 12 in-house raters, who indicated which response was more helpful or declared a tie.

why: Uses a whole existing split but gives no reason that this size is adequate or why it was chosen.

state.methods: The number of prompts (n = 600) was chosen so that, for a true win rate near 50%, the 95% confidence interval on the win rate would have a half-width of about 4 percentage points, which we considered the smallest difference worth reporting.

why: Precision target on the win-rate CI determined N.

state.methods: Owing to the exploratory nature of this study, a formal sample size calculation was not performed. Thirty patients were enrolled. Patients received oral capecitabine 1,000 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 of each 21-day cycle until progression or unacceptable toxicity.

why: Says no calculation was done and gives no other reason for 30; 'exploratory' does not explain the number.

state.methods: The sample size of this secondary analysis was fixed by the parent trial (the HEARTSTRONG trial), which enrolled 2,400 participants to detect a 20% relative reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events with 90% power; the present analysis uses the 2,217 participants with baseline echocardiography.

why: Explains N comes from the parent trial and states that trial's power basis.

state.methods: Bird counts. Point counts (10 min, 50 m radius) were carried out at 96 points distributed across 24 olive groves (4 points per grove) in Jaén province, Spain, during the breeding seasons of 2021 and 2022. Each point was visited twice per season between 07:00 and 10:30.

why: Sampling layout described without reason for the number of groves or points.

state.methods: Prior to the main survey we ran a pilot with 40 households to estimate the variance of monthly consumption. Using the pilot variance and an intra-village correlation of 0.12, a minimum detectable effect of 0.2 SD with 80% power required 72 villages with 15 households each.

why: MDE calculation using pilot variance and ICC.

state.methods: Participants were 36 older adults (65–82 y) living independently in the community, recruited through senior centres and local newspaper adverts. Inclusion required a Mini-Mental State Examination score ≥ 26 and the ability to walk 10 m without an assistive device. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the University of Groningen.

why: No sample size rationale.

state.methods: Sample size was determined by the available funding: the grant supported fMRI scanning for 30 participants at the per-hour rate of the imaging centre, so we recruited 30 and did not conduct a power analysis.

why: Resource constraint is stated explicitly as how N was set.

state.methods: We aimed for a sample size comparable to other studies using the Iowa Gambling Task in clinical populations (typically 20–40 per group) and recruited 32 patients with bipolar disorder and 32 matched controls.

why: Appeal to typical sample sizes in the literature with no rationale beyond convention (counted as false).

state.methods: Recruitment of focus group participants followed the principle of information power (Malterud et al., 2016): because the aim was narrow, participants were highly specific (all were midwives with experience of water births), and dialogue quality was strong, we judged that four focus groups with 5–7 participants each would hold sufficient information power.

why: Information-power rationale stated for the number of groups.

state.methods: A convenience sample of 150 adolescents attending two secondary schools in Ibadan completed the questionnaire during class time. Schools were chosen because of existing relationships with the research team.

why: Convenience sample; reason given is for choice of schools, not for N.

state.methods: Design and participants. This double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial was conducted at 11 centres in Germany and Austria. Adults aged 18–65 with moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis (PASI ≥ 12) were randomised 2:1 to the study drug or placebo. In total, 327 patients were randomised (218 active, 109 placebo). Randomisation was stratified by centre and prior biologic exposure and was performed centrally using an interactive web response system.

why: Detailed design, no sample size justification.

state.methods: Assuming a PASI-75 response rate of 5% with placebo and 25% with active treatment, 2:1 randomisation, 90% power and a two-sided α of 0.05, 177 patients (118 active, 59 placebo) were required. The target was increased to 210 to allow for 15% discontinuation.

why: Power calculation with assumed response rates.

state.methods: Participants: 18 experienced cyclists. Previous research using similar protocols has found significant effects of nitrate supplementation with samples of 8–12 (e.g., Lansdale et al., 2015), therefore a sample of 18 was deemed sufficient.

why: Justification is that smaller prior studies found effects; no effect size, variance or power stated (bare convention).

state.methods: Participants. An a priori power analysis in the pwr package (R) for a two-sample t-test indicated that 176 participants would give 80% power to detect d = 0.42, the meta-analytic estimate of the ego-depletion effect after bias correction, at α = .05. We therefore aimed for 180 and ended with 183 after exclusions.

why: Power analysis with meta-analytic effect size.

state.methods: We recruited 16 participants (8 female, 8 male) aged 22–41 who reported using a smartwatch daily. Each session lasted about 45 minutes and participants received a €15 voucher. We chose 16 participants to fully counterbalance the four interface conditions using a balanced Latin square.

why: Gives a design reason (a multiple of the Latin-square size) for choosing 16.

state.methods: Twelve participants (6 female, 6 male) aged 22–41 who reported using a smartwatch daily took part. Condition order was counterbalanced using a balanced Latin square. Each session lasted about 45 minutes and participants received a €15 voucher.

why: Counterbalancing is described but no reason for 12 is given.

state.methods: Sites: 20 wetland ponds in the Cotswold Water Park were selected from the 43 ponds surveyed in 2018. We chose 20 because a simulation-based power analysis using the 2018 variance in macroinvertebrate richness showed that 20 ponds (10 restored, 10 unrestored) gave 82% power to detect a difference of 5 taxa.

why: Simulation-based power analysis set the number of ponds.

state.methods: A total of 1,020 respondents aged 18+ completed the online panel survey in Poland (fieldwork 3–14 March 2023). Quotas were set for sex, age group, education and region to match Central Statistical Office population figures. Data were weighted by the same variables.

why: Quotas explain composition, not total size.

state.methods: Sample size. No power calculation was undertaken for the secondary outcomes reported here. The trial's sample size (n = 460) was calculated for the primary outcome, time to first exacerbation, as reported in the protocol paper (ref. 14).

why: States that N was set by a power calculation for the primary outcome, citing where.

state.methods: Measurements were obtained from 52 healthy volunteers. Power was calculated post hoc and found to be 0.91 for the primary comparison. Participants were seated for 15 minutes before forearm blood flow was measured by venous occlusion plethysmography.

why: Post hoc (observed) power does not explain how 52 was chosen.

state.methods: study pop: all pts w/ confirmed C. difficile infection (toxin EIA +) admitted to the two teaching hospitals, Apr 2017–Mar 2022 (n=611). pts <18y excluded. no sample size calc. data from EHR + lab system; recurrence = new + toxin within 8 wks of treatment end.

why: All cases in a window, but no reason given for the window or any sample basis ('no sample size calc').

state.methods: Sample size calculation: To estimate a sensitivity of 90% with a 95% CI of ±7%, 71 cases of confirmed tuberculosis were needed. With an expected prevalence of 20% among referred patients with presumptive TB, 355 participants were required; we planned to enrol 390.

why: Precision-based calculation for sensitivity.

state.methods: The intervention was delivered to 27 classrooms (n = 614 pupils) in the Western Cape, with 26 classrooms (n = 598) serving as waitlist controls. Schools were matched on quintile and language of instruction before randomisation.

why: No justification for number of classrooms.

state.methods: Participants. Sample size was determined using the approach recommended by Lakens (2022) for a smallest effect size of interest. We defined the SESOI as a 5-point difference on the 100-point feeling thermometer, based on the smallest difference that previous work found to predict behaviour; with an SD of 22 this corresponds to d = 0.23, and 95% power in a one-sided equivalence test required 820 participants per group.

why: SESOI-based power analysis with stated values.

state.methods: Eight healthy adult beagle dogs (4 male, 4 female) were used in a four-period crossover design with a 14-day washout. The dogs were owned by the research facility and had been used previously in non-invasive pharmacokinetic studies.

why: No reason for eight dogs.

state.methods: For the pharmacokinetic comparison, 24 subjects provide at least 80% power to conclude bioequivalence (90% CI for the geometric mean ratio of AUC within 80–125%) assuming an intra-subject CV of 20% and a true ratio of 0.95, per the standard two-period crossover calculation.

why: Bioequivalence power calculation with CV and ratio.

state.methods: We invited all 312 first-year medical students at the university to participate; 197 consented. Because the entire cohort was invited, a sample size calculation was not relevant. The questionnaire was administered online during the second week of term.

why: Explicitly states the sample is the whole cohort by design and why no calculation was needed.

state.methods: Methods. Patients (n = 88) were randomly assigned to early mobilisation or standard care after hip fracture surgery. The trial was registered prospectively (ISRCTN 00000000) and the target sample size was fixed in the registration record before the first patient was enrolled.

why: Fixing the target in a registry says when, not how, the number was chosen.

state.methods: A total of 1,000 image–caption pairs were annotated. We chose this number because pilot annotation of 150 pairs showed a hallucination rate of about 18%, and 1,000 pairs gives a 95% CI of roughly ±2.4 points around a rate of that size, enough to compare the three captioning models.

why: Pilot rate plus a precision target determined N.

state.methods: Subjects: 45 women with gestational diabetes attending the antenatal clinic at a tertiary hospital in Chennai were enrolled after informed consent and randomised to a low-glycaemic-index diet or standard dietary advice for 8 weeks. Fasting and 2-h postprandial glucose were measured weekly.

why: N only.

Method
Participants and design
The study used a 2 (mortality salience vs. dental pain) × 2 (in-group vs. out-group author) between-subjects design.
